paras: The exclusion of Black laborers from the Oklahoma State Capitol construction took place in Oklahoma City in August 1915, when white building-trades workers objected to Black men employed as common laborers on the new Capitol. The contractor agreed that only white union labor would do the unskilled work, and the Black laborers were let go. The Tulsa Star, a Black weekly, treated the episode as an affront to Black taxpayers who were helping pay for the building.

Construction of the Capitol passed to the Stewart company in early August 1915, its contract signed on Aug. 3 and work beginning the next day. Members of the Hod Carriers', Building and Common Laborers' union, an American Federation of Labor affiliate, had done practically all the work on the Capitol up to that time.

According to an Oklahoma City dispatch dated Aug. 4, the appearance of Black workers at the capitol grounds brought a committee from the local trades council to Stewart company Superintendent Rice. The dispatch repeated reports that some of the Black men had been "imported" and that they were not organized. At the conference it was agreed that white labor belonging to the union would be employed in the unskilled division, and the dispatch described a "serious labor difficulty" as having been "averted."

The Tulsa Star gave a sharper account on Aug. 27, citing "authentic reports" that the white workmen had struck "a few days ago" because Black men were employed as common laborers. In its version the Black laborers were "peremptorily dismissed" and the white workmen returned on the assurance that no Black men would be employed afterward.
No names of the dismissed laborers, and no later report of their reinstatement or of any official response, appear in the coverage.

The white dispatch, run in the Daily Ardmoreite under the headline "White Labor Will Be Used at Capitol Building," presented the outcome as a labor dispute settled in favor of union men, without comment on the Black workers beyond the reports about them. The Tulsa Star placed the episode in an editorial, "The State Capital and the Negro," calling it "a slap in the face to every negro in the state" and "the limit for injustice." Its editor argued that Black Oklahomans, who in 1910 paid taxes on property valued at $25,365,640, were entitled to a share of the money spent on the Capitol, and blamed "a few selfish, unmanly white men" for the dismissals.
The editorial ran on the Star's fourth page beside comment on the lynching of Frank in Georgia, and the page survives in several overlapping scans.

The two accounts differ on whether a strike occurred: the Aug. 4 dispatch said the difficulty was averted by agreement, while the Tulsa Star, writing three weeks later, said the white workmen struck before the Black laborers were dismissed. The dispatch is the nearer report in time and place, but the coverage does not show whether the Star described the same arrangement or a later walkout.

reader.title: Exclusion of Black laborers from the Oklahoma State Capitol construction
bases: White building-trades workers and their union objected to Black men employed as laborers on the Capitol and secured their exclusion, by a conference (A1) or a strike (A2); no physical violence is reported.

A white-press Oklahoma City dispatch (A1) and a Black-press editorial (A2) independently report that white labor's objection to Black laborers on the Capitol led to an arrangement that only white men would do the unskilled work, though they differ on whether a strike occurred.

accounts.label: Oklahoma City dispatch
accounts.gist: A serious labor difficulty over the appearance of Black workers at the capitol grounds was averted when a trades council committee met the contractor's superintendent and it was agreed that white union labor would do the unskilled work.

accounts.label: Black editor (Tulsa Star)
accounts.gist: Citing 'authentic reports', white workmen struck because Black men were employed as common laborers; the Black men were dismissed and the whites returned on assurance none would be employed hereafter.

framing.detail: Headlined 'White Labor Will Be Used at Capitol Building', the dispatch presented the outcome as a labor dispute settled, repeating reports that the Black workers were 'imported' and unorganized without comment.
The Tulsa Star editorial 'The State Capital and the Negro' called the dismissal 'a slap in the face to every negro in the state' caused by 'a few selfish, unmanly white men'.

versions.value: Difficulty 'averted' by a conference; white union labor to be used for unskilled work (no strike mentioned)
White workmen struck; Black laborers dismissed and whites returned to work

conflicts.note: The dispatch is contemporaneous and local in origin; the Tulsa Star wrote three weeks later from unnamed 'authentic reports'. They may describe the same arrangement differently or separate incidents.
If the two reports describe one episode, the Tulsa Star's timing is loose; the coverage does not settle it.
